title: Pulmonary Hypertension
subject: Pathology
summary: Pulmonary hypertension is a haemodynamic disorder with mean pulmonary arterial pressure ≥ 20 mmHg at rest. It results from vascular remodeling, left‑heart disease, lung disease, chronic thrombo‑embolism or multifactorial causes and leads to right‑heart failure.

sections.p: PH is defined by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) ≥ 20 mmHg measured by right‑heart catheterisation (RHC). The diagnosis requires exclusion of acute causes and confirmation of chronic elevation.
b: RHC is the gold standard; echocardiography is the bedside screen.
mPAP ≥ 20 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ≤ 15 mmHg for pre‑capillary PH.

t.b: Does the patient have elevated right‑systolic pressure? A tricuspid regurgitant jet ≥ 3.4 m/s suggests mPAP ≥ 20 mmHg.
What is the exact haemodynamic profile? Confirms mPAP, pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) and wedge pressure; required before targeted therapy.
Is there evidence of pulmonary artery enlargement or right‑heart enlargement? Supports PH but is non‑specific.

sections.p: Severity is graded by WHO functional class (I–IV) and by haemodynamics (PVR, cardiac output). Staging guides therapy intensity.
b: WHO‑FC I: No limitation of ordinary activity.
WHO‑FC IV: Symptoms at rest, signs of right‑heart failure.

t.b: How limited is exercise capacity? Distance < 300 m indicates severe disease.
Is right‑ventricular strain present? Levels > 300 pg/mL correlate with worse prognosis.

sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings, the most common contributors are chronic lung disease, left‑heart disease, and infections that affect the pulmonary vasculature.
b: Group 1 (PAH): HIV, connective‑tissue disease, congenital shunts.
Group 2: Rheumatic mitral stenosis, hypertensive heart disease.
Group 3: COPD, post‑TB fibrosis, chronic hypoxia from high altitude.
Group 4: Chronic thrombo‑embolic PH (CTEPH) after untreated VTE.
Group 5: Schistosomiasis, sickle‑cell disease, herbal toxins.

sections.p: Patients develop progressive dyspnoea, fatigue and peripheral oedema. Early disease may show disproportionate dyspnoea compared with spirometry.
b: Exertional dyspnoea out of proportion to lung function.
Loud P2, right‑sided S3, jugular venous distension.
Ankle swelling, hepatomegaly in advanced stages.

sections.p: A stepwise approach uses bedside tools first, then referral for definitive haemodynamic measurement.
b: Echocardiography to estimate pressure and assess right‑ventricular size.
Chest imaging to look for lung disease or pulmonary artery enlargement.
Pulmonary function tests (PFTs) to differentiate lung‑ versus heart‑origin.

t.b: Is there obstructive or restrictive lung disease? Normal FEV1/FVC with low DLCO suggests vascular disease.
Is chronic thrombo‑embolism present? Mismatched perfusion defects point to CTEPH.
Is HIV a contributing factor? Positive result moves patient to Group 1 PAH.
Is schistosomiasis present? Positive serology supports Group 5 PH in endemic areas.

sections.p: Uncontrolled PH rapidly leads to right‑heart failure and death.
b: Sudden worsening dyspnoea with syncope – possible acute decompensation.
Peripheral cyanosis, hypotension – impending right‑ventricular collapse.
Recurrent haemoptysis – may signal pulmonary artery rupture.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then add targeted therapy and supportive measures.
b: Oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxia (PaO2 < 55 mmHg or 7.3 kPa).
Diuretics for right‑sided fluid overload.
Anticoagulation if CTEPH or recurrent VTE is confirmed.
Endothelin‑receptor antagonists (e.g., bosentan) for Group 1 PAH – reduce vasoconstriction.
Phosphodiesterase‑5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil) – improve nitric‑oxide pathway.
Avoid calcium‑channel blockers unless vasoreactivity test is positive.

sections.p: Regular clinical review, functional class assessment and repeat echocardiography guide therapy escalation.
b: Clinic review every 3–6 months; earlier if symptoms change.
Repeat 6MWT and NT‑proBNP to track progression.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce respiratory infections.
Left‑sided heart failure – both cause dyspnoea, but left‑sided failure shows pulmonary crackles and elevated wedge pressure.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease – COPD has obstructive spirometry and smoking history; PH has normal spirometry early.
Pulmonary embolism – acute onset, pleuritic chest pain, and CT pulmonary angiography differentiate.
Normal echocardiographic pressure estimate in early disease – RHC may still reveal elevated mPAP.
Low NT‑proBNP in obese patients – may mask right‑ventricular strain.
Chest X‑ray may appear normal despite severe PH.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid increase in leg swelling with abdominal distension

faq.q: Why is right‑heart catheterisation required before starting PAH‑specific drugs?
faq.a: It confirms the haemodynamic definition, distinguishes pre‑ from post‑capillary PH and avoids treating left‑heart disease with inappropriate vasodilators.

faq.q: Can long‑term oxygen therapy improve survival?
faq.a: Yes, in chronic hypoxic PH it reduces pulmonary vasoconstriction and improves survival when used ≥15 hours daily.

faq.q: Is PH curable in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Cure is rare; control of the underlying cause (e.g., treating HIV, repairing a shunt) and symptom management can markedly improve quality of life.

exam: A 35‑year‑old woman with HIV presents with exertional dyspnoea; echo shows TR jet 3.6 m/s. What is the next diagnostic step and why? — Right‑heart catheterisation to confirm pre‑capillary PH and guide therapy.

A patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis develops PH. How does the underlying mechanism differ from PAH? — Elevated left‑atrial pressure raises wedge pressure (post‑capillary PH), so vasodilators are contraindicated.
In a rural clinic you cannot perform RHC. Which bedside test helps risk‑stratify and what threshold indicates severe disease? — 6‑minute walk distance <300 m suggests severe PH.
Why is a calcium‑channel blocker not first‑line for most PH patients? — Only a small subset shows acute vasoreactivity; indiscriminate use can cause systemic hypotension.
A patient on sildenafil develops worsening oedema. What should you do? — Review for right‑heart failure; add diuretic and consider switching to an endothelin‑receptor antagonist.

How does chronic schistosomiasis cause PH and what specific investigation confirms it? — Egg‑induced portal hypertension leads to pulmonary vascular remodeling; serology or stool microscopy confirms infection.
What red‑flag symptom mandates immediate hospital admission in PH? — New syncope or rapid progression of right‑sided heart failure signs.

Explain why anticoagulation is recommended in chronic thrombo‑embolic PH but not in isolated PAH. — CTEPH involves persistent thrombus; anticoagulation prevents further emboli, whereas PAH risk of bleeding outweighs benefit.
